lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Weld testing and quality control are not optional extrasâthey are what separate a paid welder from a rework welder. In Africa, where a single failed weld on a water tank, truck chassis, or gate can mean lost income and damaged reputation, testing your work is how you stay in business. A weld that looks good can still be weak inside. Porosity, lack of fusion, and undercut are invisible to the eye but will fail under load. You must test.

Start with visual inspection (VT). It is free, fast, and catches about 80% of defects. Use a bright torch, a magnifying glass (10x), and a weld gauge set. Check for cracks, undercut deeper than 0.5 mm, overlap, and spatter. Measure leg length on fillet weldsâif you specified 6 mm, and it is 4 mm, that weld is 33% weaker. On butt welds, check reinforcement height: it should not exceed 3 mm. Too high creates a stress riser; too low means underfill.

Beyond visual, you have destructive and non-destructive testing (NDT). Destructive tests like bend tests and nick-break tests are cheap and common in training. Cut a coupon, bend it in a vice or press. If the weld opens up, you had lack of fusion or slag inclusion. Non-destructive tests include dye penetrant (PT) for surface cracks, magnetic particle (MT) for surface and near-surface defects in steel, ultrasonic (UT) for internal flaws, and radiographic (RT) for critical jobs. In most African workshops, PT and MT are affordable; UT and RT are for high-value work like pressure vessels or structural steel for bridges.

Quality control also means documentation. Keep a weld map: who welded what, when, with which electrode, and what tests were done. If a client complains, you can trace the problem. Use a checklist: pre-weld (material grade, joint prep, fit-up), during weld (amps, travel speed, interpass temperature), post-weld (visual, dimensional, NDT if required).

Finally, remember: testing is not about catching youâit is about proving your skill. A welder who tests and documents gets repeat contracts. A welder who guesses gets callbacks. Start testing today with a simple bend test on your next practice coupon. You will learn more from one broken test than from ten perfect-looking welds.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To test welds properly, you need a basic kit that costs less than a cheap grinder. Start with visual inspection tools: a bright LED torch (at least 200 lumens), a 10x magnifying glass, a weld fillet gauge (measures leg length and throat), an undercut gauge, and a steel ruler. A cheap digital caliper (0â150 mm) is also useful. For dye penetrant testing (PT), buy a three-part kit: cleaner, penetrant (red), and developer (white). A 500 ml kit costs around $20â30 and does many tests. For magnetic particle testing (MT), you need a yoke (AC or permanent magnet), black iron powder or fluorescent powder, and a UV lamp if using fluorescent. A basic yoke costs $50â100; powder is cheap.

For destructive tests, you need a vice, a hammer (2â4 kg), a hacksaw or abrasive chop saw, and a bend test jig. You can make a bend jig from two pieces of 50 mm pipe welded to a base. For nick-break tests, a chisel and hammer work. For macro etch, you need nitric acid (10% in water) or a commercial etchant, a plastic tray, and gloves. Always store acid in a locked cabinet.

For ultrasonic testing (UT), you need a UT flaw detector and probes (typically 2â5 MHz). These are expensive ($2,000+), so most small workshops hire a technician. Radiographic testing (RT) requires X-ray or gamma-ray equipment and is done by certified firms. In Africa, many countries have NDT service companies in major citiesâuse them for critical welds.

Consumables: grinding discs (for surface prep), wire brushes, acetone or cleaner, and marking pens. For PT, you also need lint-free rags. For MT, you need a demagnetizer if the part will be machined later.

Safety gear: gloves (nitrile for chemicals, leather for handling), safety glasses, and a respirator for acid fumes. Keep a first aid kit with burn gel and eye wash.

Where to buy: In Nigeria, check Ladipo market or online at Jumia for basic tools. In Kenya, River Road in Nairobi. In South Africa, Bearing Man Group or Adendorff. For NDT consumables, contact local NDT societies or import from China via Alibaba. Start with visual and PTâthey cover most needs. Add MT when you do structural steel. UT and RT are for specialized jobs; partner with a certified inspector rather than buying equipment.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Follow this sequence for a complete weld quality check. First, clean the weld. Remove slag, spatter, and dirt with a wire brush and grinder. The weld must be bare metal. For visual inspection, use a torch at a low angle to cast shadowsâdefects like undercut and cracks show up as dark lines. Check the entire length, including start and stop points. Measure leg length on fillets with a gauge: for a 6 mm fillet, the gauge should touch both plates. If it rocks, the leg is too small. Check for undercut with a gauge; anything over 0.5 mm on a 6 mm plate is a defect. Record your findings.

For dye penetrant testing (PT), follow these steps: 1) Pre-clean with cleaner and let dry. 2) Spray penetrant and wait 10â15 minutes (dwell time). 3) Wipe off excess with a clean rag, then clean with cleanerâdo not spray cleaner directly on the part; spray on the rag. 4) Spray developer and wait 10â15 minutes. 5) Inspect under bright light. Red lines or dots indicate defects. Mark them. 6) Clean off developer with cleaner. PT works on any non-porous material.

For magnetic particle testing (MT), only for ferromagnetic materials (steel, iron). 1) Clean the surface. 2) Apply black iron powder (dry) or wet suspension. 3) Magnetize the part with a yokeâplace the legs on either side of the weld, press the trigger, and move slowly. 4) Look for powder buildup (indications) while magnetizing. 5) Turn off, clean, and repeat in two directions (90Â° apart) to catch all orientations. 6) Demagnetize if needed. MT finds surface and near-surface defects.

For a bend test (destructive), cut a coupon across the weld, grind the weld flush, and bend it in a jig. The weld should stretch to a U-shape without opening. If it cracks, you have lack of fusion or slag. For a nick-break test, cut a notch along the weld, then break it with a hammer. Inspect the fracture face for porosity, slag, or incomplete fusion.

After testing, document: weld ID, test method, result, and inspector name. If a defect is found, mark it, grind it out, and re-weld. Re-test. Never paint over a defect.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Testing only with a visual check. Visual misses internal defects. Fix: Add dye penetrant (PT) for surface cracks and magnetic particle (MT) for near-surface defects on steel. For critical welds, use ultrasonic (UT) or radiographic (RT).

Mistake 2: Not cleaning before PT. Oil, grease, or paint block penetrant. Fix: Clean with solvent, then let dry. Use a wire brush and grinder to remove scale. If you skip this, you get false passes.

Mistake 3: Wrong dwell time for PT. Too short (under 5 minutes) means penetrant doesn't seep into defects; too long (over 30 minutes) makes it dry out. Fix: Follow the kit instructionsâusually 10â15 minutes. Set a timer.

Mistake 4: Using the wrong current for MT. AC finds surface defects; DC finds deeper ones. Fix: For general welds, use AC yoke. For critical, use DC. Also, magnetize in two directionsâif you only do one, you miss defects perpendicular to the field.

Mistake 5: Misreading indications. Not every red dot is a crack. Fix: Verify with a magnifying glass. If unsure, grind and re-test. A false call wastes time; a missed defect costs lives.

Mistake 6: Skipping calibration. Your gauge or caliper may be off. Fix: Check zero before use. For UT, calibrate on a reference block daily.

Mistake 7: Testing after painting. Paint hides defects and interferes with PT/MT. Fix: Test before painting. If you must test painted parts, use UT or RT.

Mistake 8: No documentation. If you don't record, you can't prove quality. Fix: Keep a logbook with date, weld ID, test method, result, and your name. Take photos.

Mistake 9: Using expired chemicals. Old penetrant or developer gives poor results. Fix: Check expiry dates. Store in a cool, dark place.

Mistake 10: Not re-testing after repair. Fix: Any repaired weld must be re-tested with the same method. Never assume it's good.

Mistake 11: Ignoring safety. PT chemicals are flammable and toxic. Fix: Wear nitrile gloves, safety glasses, and work in a ventilated area. No smoking.

Mistake 12: Over-testing cheap jobs. Not every weld needs UT. Fix: Match test method to criticality. For a gate, visual is enough. For a pressure vessel, use RT.

Fix these mistakes and your weld rejection rate will drop. Test smart, not just hard.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Weld testing involves chemicals, radiation, and heavy equipmentâsafety is not optional. Start with personal protective equipment (PPE). For visual inspection, wear safety glasses and gloves. For dye penetrant (PT), use nitrile gloves (not latexâpenetrant eats through latex), safety glasses, and a respirator with organic vapor cartridges if working indoors. PT chemicals are flammableâkeep away from welding arcs and sparks. Store in a locked metal cabinet. For magnetic particle (MT) with dry powder, wear a dust mask. With wet suspension, avoid skin contact. For ultrasonic (UT), no special PPE beyond gloves, but the couplant can irritate skinâwash after use. For radiographic (RT), only certified personnel should be near the source. If you hire an RT crew, clear the area and wear dosimeters.

Best practice 1: Test before you paint. Paint hides defects and ruins PT/MT. If you must test painted parts, use UT or RT.

Best practice 2: Use a checklist. Pre-test: clean, dry, and check equipment calibration. During test: follow dwell times, magnetize in two directions, and inspect under good light. Post-test: clean chemicals off, document, and mark defects.

Best practice 3: Never test alone. Have a second person verify your findings. Two pairs of eyes catch more.

Best practice 4: Keep a logbook. Record weld ID, test method, result, and date. This protects you if a client complains.

Best practice 5: Dispose of chemicals properly. PT penetrant and developer are hazardous waste. Do not pour down drains. Collect in a sealed container and take to a licensed disposal site. In many African cities, local environmental agencies can advise.

Best practice 6: Train regularly. NDT methods have standards (ASME, AWS, ISO). Take a short course or watch reputable YouTube tutorials. Practice on scrap until you can reliably detect a 0.5 mm crack.

Best practice 7: Know your limits. If a job requires UT or RT, hire a certified inspector. Do not fake it. A failed bridge or pressure vessel can kill.

Best practice 8: Maintain your tools. Clean gauges, store PT kits upright, and check batteries in UV lamps. A dirty lens or dead battery can cause a missed defect.

Best practice 9: Work in a ventilated area. PT and MT chemicals release fumes. Open windows or use a fan. If you smell strong solvent, increase ventilation.

Best practice 10: First aid. Keep burn gel, eye wash, and a first aid kit nearby. If chemicals get in your eyes, flush with water for 15 minutes and seek medical help.

Safety is not a costâit is an investment in your reputation and your life.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
This exercise will teach you to test a fillet weld using visual inspection and dye penetrant testing (PT). You will need: two steel plates (100 mm x 50 mm x 6 mm), a welder, E6013 or E7018 electrodes, a grinder, wire brush, dye penetrant kit (cleaner, penetrant, developer), a fillet gauge, a magnifying glass, and gloves. Work in a ventilated area.

Step 1: Prepare and weld. Clean the plates. Tack weld them in a T-joint. Weld a 100 mm fillet on one side using 3.2 mm electrode at 90â110 amps. Let it cool. Remove slag with a chisel and wire brush. Grind the weld lightly to remove spatter but do not grind the weld itself.

Step 2: Visual inspection. Use a torch at a low angle. Check for undercut, overlap, cracks, and spatter. Measure leg length with a fillet gaugeâit should be 6 mm. If not, note it. Check for undercut with a gauge; anything over 0.5 mm is a defect. Record your findings in a logbook.

Step 3: Dye penetrant testing. 1) Clean the weld and surrounding 25 mm with cleaner. Let dry. 2) Spray penetrant and wait 15 minutes. 3) Wipe off excess with a clean rag, then spray cleaner on the rag and wipe again. Do not spray cleaner directly on the part. 4) Spray developer and wait 15 minutes. 5) Inspect under bright light with a magnifying glass. Red lines or dots indicate defects. Mark them with a marker. 6) Clean off developer with cleaner.

Step 4: Destructive test (optional). Cut a 25 mm coupon across the weld. Bend it in a vice or bend jig. If it cracks, inspect the fracture for slag or lack of fusion. If it bends without cracking, your weld passes.

Step 5: Repair and re-test. If you found defects, grind them out completely (until you see clean metal) and re-weld. Re-test with PT. Document the repair.

Step 6: Write a report. Include: date, welder name, electrode type, amps, visual findings, PT findings, and pass/fail. Take a photo of the tested weld.

Repeat this exercise three times with different amperages (e.g., 80 A, 100 A, 120 A). See how amperage affects defect formation. At too low amps, you get lack of fusion; at too high, undercut and spatter. This teaches you to set your machine correctly. By the end, you will have a repeatable quality control routine that you can use on real jobs. Remember: test, document, repair, re-test.

quiz.q: What is the most common and cost-effective weld test?
quiz.explanation: Visual inspection is free, fast, and catches about 80% of defects.

quiz.q: Which test uses a red penetrant and white developer?
quiz.explanation: Dye penetrant testing uses a colored penetrant and a developer to draw it out.

quiz.q: What is the maximum allowed undercut depth on a 6 mm plate?
quiz.explanation: Undercut deeper than 0.5 mm is considered a defect on a 6 mm plate.

quiz.q: Which test is only for ferromagnetic materials?
quiz.explanation: Magnetic particle testing works only on steel and iron because it relies on magnetism.

quiz.q: What is the typical dwell time for dye penetrant before wiping?
quiz.explanation: Penetrant needs 10â15 minutes to seep into defects.

quiz.q: Which tool measures fillet weld leg length?
quiz.explanation: A fillet gauge directly measures leg length and throat thickness.

quiz.q: What does a bend test check for?
options: B) Internal defects like lack of fusion
quiz.explanation: Bend tests reveal internal defects by stressing the weld until it opens or stretches.

quiz.q: Which NDT method uses a yoke?
quiz.explanation: A yoke is used to magnetize the part in magnetic particle testing.

quiz.q: What should you do before dye penetrant testing?
options: B) Clean the weld with solvent
D) Cool the weld with water
quiz.explanation: The surface must be clean and dry so penetrant can enter defects.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when using PT?
quiz.explanation: Oil, grease, or paint block penetrant and cause false results.

quiz.q: Which test is best for internal defects in a thick weld?
quiz.explanation: Ultrasonic testing can detect internal flaws deep within the weld.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a developer in PT?
options: B) To draw penetrant out of defects
quiz.explanation: Developer acts as a blotter to pull penetrant out so defects become visible.

quiz.q: Which PPE is essential for dye penetrant testing?
quiz.explanation: Nitrile gloves protect skin from chemicals; latex is not resistant.

quiz.q: What does a nick-break test reveal?
quiz.explanation: Breaking a notched weld exposes internal defects on the fracture face.

quiz.q: How many directions should you magnetize in MT?
quiz.explanation: Magnetizing in two directions (90Â° apart) catches defects of all orientations.

quiz.q: What is the maximum reinforcement height for a butt weld?
quiz.explanation: Excessive reinforcement (over 3 mm) creates a stress riser.

quiz.q: Which test requires a certified technician and radiation safety?
quiz.explanation: Radiographic testing uses X-rays or gamma rays and requires certification.

quiz.q: What should you do after finding a defect?
options: B) Grind it out and re-weld
D) Add more weld on top
quiz.explanation: Defects must be completely removed and re-welded, then re-tested.

quiz.q: Why is documentation important in weld testing?
options: B) To trace problems and prove quality
quiz.explanation: Records allow traceability and demonstrate that quality standards were met.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when using MT?
options: A) Using AC instead of DC
B) Not magnetizing in two directions
quiz.explanation: One direction misses defects perpendicular to the magnetic field.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used in macro etch testing?
quiz.explanation: A 10% nitric acid solution etches the weld to reveal internal structure.

quiz.q: What is the first step in visual inspection?
quiz.explanation: The weld must be clean and bare metal for defects to be visible.

quiz.q: What does a fillet gauge measure?
quiz.explanation: A fillet gauge checks leg length and throat thickness against specifications.

quiz.q: Which test is best for detecting surface cracks in aluminum?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum is non-ferromagnetic, so MT won't work; PT detects surface cracks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a bend test jig?
options: A) To hold the coupon while bending
quiz.explanation: A jig provides controlled bending to test weld ductility.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after spraying developer before inspecting?
quiz.explanation: Developer needs 10â15 minutes to draw penetrant out for inspection.

quiz.q: What is a sign of lack of fusion in a bend test?
options: B) Crack or opening along the weld
quiz.explanation: Lack of fusion causes the weld to open or crack when bent.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a non-destructive test?
quiz.explanation: Bend test is destructive because it permanently deforms the coupon.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a false indication in PT?
quiz.explanation: Grinding removes the surface and allows re-testing to confirm if a defect exists.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important during PT?
options: A) To dry the part faster
B) To avoid inhaling toxic fumes
quiz.explanation: PT chemicals release harmful vapors that require fresh air circulation.
